terrestrial

/tuh-RES-tree-ul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Terrestrial means relating to or living on land, as opposed to in water or in the air.

Kiwis are among the most thoroughly terrestrial of all birds, nesting and feeding entirely on the forest floor.

Example

A zoologist sorting a museum's snail drawers applies one simple test: does the animal breathe with a lung or with a gill? The lunged snails cannot breathe under water at all, and they crawl over leaf litter, seal themselves against dry weather, and drown if held under for long. The gilled ones cannot survive a single day out of the pond. The lunged half of the collection goes into a drawer labelled terrestrial.

Snails that breathe air, crawl over leaf litter, and drown if held under water belong entirely to the land, and terrestrial is the word for land-living.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

land-dwelling: Land-dwelling states where an animal makes its home and nothing more. Terrestrial says that of animals too, but stretches much further -- terrestrial ecosystems, terrestrial planets, terrestrial broadcasting -- wherever land or the ground itself is the point.

ground-based: Ground-based describes equipment and operations run from the ground rather than from the air or from orbit -- a ground-based telescope, ground-based radar. Terrestrial is the naturalist's word for life that belongs to land rather than to water or the air.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

arboreal: living in trees

marine: living in the sea

Where it sits · how strictly confined to dry ground — land-based → terrestrial → land-bound

land-based vs. terrestrial: Land-based describes where an operation or force is stationed -- land-based missiles, a land-based air fleet -- rather than where a creature naturally lives, which is the claim terrestrial makes.

land-bound vs. terrestrial: Land-bound is stronger, suggesting an animal cannot leave the land at all, while a terrestrial animal may still swim a river or climb a tree from time to time.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — terr-

Root — terr-: earth, land (Latin terra)

Suffix — -estrial

Suffix — -estrial: belonging to; of the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Latin terra meant the dry land, as opposed to sea and sky, and terrestris meant 'of the land.' English uses the word for animals of the ground, for broadcasting sent through the air from ground masts, and, with extra- added, for anything from beyond our planet. The same terra underlies territory, terrain, and subterranean.

Use the root in a new word: extraterrestrial

Use the root in a new word: extraterrestrial: The radio telescope sweeps the sky all night for any extraterrestrial signal worth a second listen.

Word Choice

scientific; also used of broadcasting

Terrestrial contrasts with life in water and life in the air, and in broadcasting it means transmitted from the ground rather than by satellite. Its water-side counterpart in this unit is aquatic, and an animal that genuinely divides its life between the two is neither one nor the other but amphibious.
